propositions.text: Applicant challenges CIC decision denying him a Temporary Resident Permit dated January 16, 2016.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Ayodeji Akanmu Alabi [Mr. Alabi], challenges a Citizenship and Immigration Canada [CIC] decision dated January 16, 2016, which denied him a Temporary Resident Permit [TRP].

propositions.text: Applicant was removed to Nigeria on June 5, 2015, despite long history with Canadian immigration system since 1998.
propositions.quote: Mr. Alabi was removed to Nigeria on June 5, 2015, despite having a long history with our immigration system and living here since January 17, 1998.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant challenges a January 16, 2016 CIC decision denying a TRP and notes his removal to Nigeria in 2015 despite long Canadian residence.

propositions.text: Applicant seeks mandamus order directing issuance of TRP nunc pro tunc to initial refusal date and re-entry facilitation within 30 days.
propositions.quote: Mr. Alabi seeks an order of mandamus directing the Respondent’s officials to issue a TRP nunc pro tunc to the date of his initial refusal. He requests an order requiring the Respondent to facilitate his re-entry into Canada no later than thirty days from the date of this decision.

propositions.text: Applicant no longer seeks costs.
propositions.quote: Mr. Alabi is no longer seeking costs.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant seeks mandamus for TRP issuance and re-entry facilitation but no longer seeks costs, as he submits.

propositions.text: Court will grant judicial review but not the relief sought; matter remitted for re-determination by different officer.
propositions.quote: I will grant the application for judicial review; however, I will not grant the relief that is sought by Mr. Alabi. This matter will be sent back to be re-determined by a different officer for the reasons that follow.

paragraphs.summary: The court grants judicial review but denies the relief sought and remits the matter for re-determination by a different officer.

propositions.text: Applicant is Nigerian citizen in common law relationship with Canadian citizen for 16 years, has five children, runs Toronto business, involved in community.
propositions.quote: Mr. Alabi is a citizen of Nigeria. He has been in an ongoing common law relationship with a Canadian citizen for sixteen years, has five children, operates a successful Toronto business, and had been heavily involved in his community.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant is a Nigerian citizen in a 16-year common law relationship with a Canadian, has five children, a business, and community involvement.

propositions.text: Applicant pled guilty and was convicted in US in 1993 for conspiracy to distribute heroin, sentenced to 24 months.
propositions.quote: On May 11, 1993, Mr. Alabi pled guilty to and was convicted in the United States [US] of conspiracy to distribute heroin. ... He was sentenced to 24 months in jail.

propositions.text: Conflicting conviction date noted as 1995 but 1993 used as it does not affect application.
propositions.quote: There is conflicting information in the Applicant’s material concerning the date of conviction as it is also noted as May 11, 1995. Nothing in this application turns on this discrepancy so 1993 will be used.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found the applicant pled guilty in 1993 to heroin conspiracy and was sentenced to 24 months, despite conflicting date noted.

propositions.text: Applicant deported from US, came to Canada in 1998, refugee claim refused in 1999, H&C application refused, found inadmissible in 2007 with deportation and exclusion orders.
propositions.quote: After being deported from the US, Mr. Alabi came to Canada in 1998 and made an application for refugee status. His refugee claim was refused in April 1999. His subsequent humanitarian and compassionate relief [H&C] application was also refused. On April 17, 2007, the Immigration Division found Mr. Alabi inadmissible to Canada based on serious criminality and misrepresentation, issuing a deportation order and a concurrent exclusion order.

propositions.text: Federal Court refused leave and judicial review of these decisions.
propositions.quote: Application for leave and judicial review of both these decisions was refused by the Federal Court.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found applicant deported from US, refugee and H&C claims refused, inadmissible in 2007, with Federal Court refusing review.

propositions.text: Applicant's criminal rehabilitation application refused in 2012; judicial review refused; second H&C application submitted in 2009 still under review.
propositions.quote: Mr. Alabi then submitted a criminal rehabilitation application to CIC which was refused on May 4, 2012. Application for leave and judicial review of this decision was also refused. A second H&C application was submitted on April 20, 2009. This application is still under review by CIC some eight years later.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found applicant's 2012 criminal rehabilitation refused with refused judicial review; second H&C application from 2009 still under review.

propositions.text: Second criminal rehabilitation application refused in 2013; judicial review refused; third rehabilitation application submitted in 2014 and still under review in 2016.
propositions.quote: A second criminal rehabilitation application was submitted by Mr. Alabi on October 2, 2012. The second rehabilitation application was refused on October 24, 2013, as was the application for leave for judicial review. A third criminal rehabilitation application was submitted on January 21, 2014, and was transferred to the Canadian High Commission in Lagos, Nigeria in 2016. This third rehabilitation application is also still under review.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found second criminal rehabilitation refused in 2013 with refused review; third application submitted in 2014 still under review in 2016.

propositions.text: Duplicate second H&C application filed in 2012; no spousal sponsorship application received by CIC; outstanding H&C and rehabilitation applications exist.
propositions.quote: A duplicate of Mr. Alabi’s second H&C application was filed on October 2, 2012. Contrary to Mr. Alabi’s belief, CIC has not received a spousal sponsorship application. CIC does, however, have the outstanding H&C and rehabilitation applications.

paragraphs.summary: The court states a duplicate second H&C application was filed in 2012; no spousal sponsorship received; outstanding H&C and rehabilitation applications remain.

propositions.text: Applicant's TRP application in 2015 refused; judicial review led to re-determination by consent; motion for contempt dismissed; applicant removed June 5, 2015; TRP re-determined and refused in 2016.
propositions.quote: Mr. Alabi submitted a TRP application on February 5, 2015, which was refused; however, on judicial review, the parties agreed to a re-determination by way of consent judgment. Mr. Alabi then brought a motion to hold the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration personally in contempt of court for the closed file, which was dismissed. Mr. Alabi was removed from Canada on June 5, 2015. On January 13, 2016, Mr. Alabi’s TRP was re-determined and refused. The case before me is a judicial review of this re-determined TRP application.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found applicant's 2015 TRP refused, re-determined by consent, contempt motion dismissed, removal in 2015, and 2016 TRP refusal under review.

propositions.text: CIC's reasons for TRP refusal were brief and in point form, citing applicant's reason to attend daughter's US convocation requiring durable immigration status.
propositions.quote: CIC’s reasons for refusing Mr. Alabi’s TRP are very brief and in point form. The reasons given are that Mr. Alabi’s application indicates that the reason for his TRP is so he can attend his daughter’s convocation in the US.

propositions.text: Applicant alleged US consulate requires durable Canadian or US immigration status for visitor visa; daughters and step-daughter submitted letters in support.
propositions.quote: He alleges that to do so, he must have “durable immigration status in Canada, [or] the US consulate will not issue a visitor visa”. Mr. Alabi’s daughters and step-daughter submitted letters in support of his TRP application.

propositions.text: No evidence from law school or medical school confirming convocations; no supporting documentation from US consulate or immigration provided.
propositions.quote: No evidence from her law school was presented to confirm this. A letter from Mr. Alabi’s step-daughter ... was addressed from a medical school in St. Kitts ... no confirmation from this university was provided either. Mr. Alabi did not provide supporting documentation from the US consulate or US immigration to satisfy the officer of this claim.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found CIC gave brief reasons citing applicant's reason to attend daughter's US convocation, but no confirming evidence or US consulate documentation was provided.

propositions.text: Applicant owns business in Canada but did not satisfy officer on impact of absence; officer unsatisfied on community impact; overall insufficient reasons to justify TRP issuance.
propositions.quote: Mr. Alabi indicated he owns and operates a business in Canada but did not satisfy the officer as to how his absence from Canada would impact the business. The officer was equally unsatisfied as to how his absence would impact any community organizations that he had been a member of or supported. Overall, the officer was not satisfied that there were sufficient reasons to justify the issuance of a TRP and Mr. Alabi’s application was correspondingly refused.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found applicant failed to satisfy officer on business or community impact; officer refused TRP for insufficient reasons.

propositions.text: Standard of review is reasonableness; decision must be within a range of acceptable outcomes defensible on facts and law (Dunsmuir).
propositions.quote: The applicable standard of review to the issue in this case is that of reasonableness and the decision must fall “within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and law” (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 47 [Dunsmuir]).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review is reasonableness per Dunsmuir, requiring decisions to be defensible on facts and law.

propositions.text: Applicant argues officer breached duty to give reasons by omitting important factors in immigration record (citing Turner and Via Rail).
propositions.quote: Mr. Alabi submits that the officer breached his duty to give reasons because he did not mention the important factors that were clearly in his immigration record (Turner v Canada (Attorney General), 2012 FCA 159 at paras 40-42; Via Rail Canada Inc v National Transportation Agency, [2001] 2 FC 25 at para 22).

propositions.text: Respondent argues TRP granting is exceptional; succinct reasons suffice to inform applicant and respond to scant submissions.
propositions.quote: However, the Respondent counters that the granting of a TRP is exceptional and the reasons, though succinct, allow Mr. Alabi to understand why the TRP was refused and responds directly to his “scant” submissions and evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues officer breached duty to give reasons; respondent counters succinct reasons suffice given exceptional nature and scant submissions.

propositions.text: Inadequacy of reasons alone is not basis to set aside decision; reasons must be examined in context of reasonableness (Newfoundland Nurses).
propositions.quote: The Supreme Court of Canada, in Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses’ Union v Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62 [Newfoundland Nurses], established that the inadequacy of reasons is not a stand-alone basis for setting aside a decision. Rather, the reasons should be examined in the context of whether the outcome of the decision is reasonable.

propositions.text: Reasons need not include every argument or case; court must understand why decision was made and if result meets Dunsmuir criteria.
propositions.quote: Reasons do not need to include every argument, provision, or case in order to be found reasonable and valid. Simply put, the Court must be able to understand from the reasons why the decision was made and whether the result meets the Dunsmuir, above, criteria.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Newfoundland Nurses that inadequate reasons alone do not invalidate decisions; reasons must show why decision was made and meet reasonableness.

propositions.text: Issue is whether the decision is reasonable.
propositions.quote: The issue to be determined is whether this decision is reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue is whether the decision is reasonable.

propositions.text: Concern that officer did not consider major factors like applicant's family unity and outstanding H&C and rehabilitation applications.
propositions.quote: The concern in this case is that the officer did not consider all of the major factors at issue such as the Applicant’s wish for him and his wife of sixteen years to be united as well as to see his children. Furthermore, no consideration is given to the materials contained in Mr. Alabi’s outstanding H&C and rehabilitation applications.

propositions.text: Officer made determination quickly relying only on narrow submissions by self-represented applicant; re-determination should consider entire factual situation.
propositions.quote: The officer came to his determination within a very short time period relying solely on the very narrow submissions presented by Mr. Alabi as a self-represented applicant. Given that the TRP application before the Court now was as a result of a re-determination after the Federal Court sent it back, I would expect the reasons this time to indicate that Mr. Alabi’s entire factual situation was considered.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer failed to consider major factors and relied narrowly on submissions; re-determination should consider entire factual situation.

propositions.text: Onus is on applicant to present compelling evidence for TRP; officer assesses if compelling reasons exist and may stop if none found (Farhat).
propositions.quote: As noted by the Respondent, the onus is on Mr. Alabi to present compelling evidence as to why a TRP should be granted, even if he is inadmissible. The Respondent submits that the officer must assess whether there are “compelling reasons” for Mr. Alabi to enter Canada; if the officer finds that is not the case, he is not required to continue the assessment (Farhat v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 1275 at para 22).

paragraphs.summary: The respondent submits the applicant bears the onus to present compelling evidence for TRP; officer may stop assessment if no compelling reasons found.

propositions.text: Applicant reasonably did not resubmit all information from other applications, unaware departments do not share all information.
propositions.quote: Mr. Alabi quite reasonably did not believe he needed to resubmit in detail all of the information contained in his other two applications as to why he wants to return to Canada. All of his immigration matters are about him and he never considered that one department did not share all his information with the officer that was making the decision from another department.

propositions.text: Given re-determination, court questions why officer used only partial information from CIC system and ignored rest.
propositions.quote: However, given that the TRP application was sent back for re-determination, I question why only a portion of the information regarding Mr. Alabi’s immigration proceedings in CIC’s system such as dates and immigration history was used by the officer and yet the rest ignored.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds applicant reasonably did not resubmit all info; questions why officer ignored much CIC information in re-determination.

propositions.text: Affidavit from CIC Case Processing Centre detailed applicant's immigration history; officer must consider major factors like 16-year relationship and outstanding H&C application.
propositions.quote: The Respondent filed an affidavit from CIC’s Case Processing Centre which gave a detailed description of Mr. Alabi’s long immigration history. The officer assessing the TRP application does not have to list every piece of history in their reasons, but I find it was unreasonable for the officer to ignore this information in its entirety. I would expect at the very least that the sixteen year relationship with his wife, and the outstanding eight year old H&C application, would be major factors to be considered.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it unreasonable for the officer to ignore detailed immigration history and major factors like long relationship and outstanding H&C application.

propositions.text: The officer only considered Mr. Alabi's brief application referring to future events.
propositions.quote: All that the officer considered was the contents of Mr. Alabi’s brief application which only referred to the new events that were coming up in the future.

propositions.text: The onus is on Mr. Alabi to present compelling reasons.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent that the onus is on Mr. Alabi to present compelling reasons;

propositions.text: It is unreasonable to think Mr. Alabi would have sent copies of his H&C and rehabilitation applications with his TRP application given unique facts.
propositions.quote: given these unique facts, it is unreasonable to think that Mr. Alabi would have thought to send a copy of his H&C and rehabilitation applications with his TRP application.

propositions.text: The officer's determination was made in isolation of Mr. Alabi's actual situation after Federal Court directed re-determination.
propositions.quote: The officer’s determination was done in complete isolation of the actual situation of Mr. Alabi, after being directed by the Federal Court to re-determine the matter.

paragraphs.summary: The officer considered only Mr. Alabi's brief application; the respondent says onus is on him; the court finds it unreasonable to expect more and that the officer ignored his situation.

propositions.text: Mr. Alabi says the officer was selective in evidence use and dismissal.
propositions.quote: Mr. Alabi says the officer was selective in what evidence it used and what it dismissed

propositions.text: The court agrees the officer was selective in evidence consideration.
propositions.quote: and I agree.

propositions.text: In Rudder, Justice Lemieux said an officer errs by failing to consider relevant factors in discretion.
propositions.quote: Justice Lemieux, when dealing with a negative TRP case, said it best in Rudder v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2009 FC 689 at para 33 [Rudder]: “Another way of putting it, the officer’s error is the failure to take into account relevant factors in the exercise of his/her discretion.”

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Alabi argues the officer was selective; the court agrees and cites Rudder on failure to consider relevant factors as error.

propositions.text: Reliance on other applications is not normally grounds for review.
propositions.quote: Reliance on other applications would not normally constitute grounds for review

propositions.text: Given Mr. Alabi's ongoing relationship with CIC, self-representation, and Federal Court remand, CIC should have reviewed all major factors for and against him.
propositions.quote: although given the ongoing relationship between Mr. Alabi and CIC, the fact he was self-represented, and the fact this was a decision sent back for redetermination from the Federal Court, CIC should have included a review of all major factors that weigh both for and against Mr. Alabi.

propositions.text: This requirement is unique to these facts and not suggested for other TRP applications.
propositions.quote: This is unique to these facts and of course I am not suggesting that is the case in other TRP applications.

paragraphs.summary: Normally reliance on other applications isn't reviewable, but here CIC should have reviewed all factors due to unique facts; not a general rule.

propositions.text: Some fault for administrative breakdown lies with Mr. Alabi due to sparse submissions and evidence.
propositions.quote: Some of the fault for this administrative breakdown belongs to Mr. Alabi as his submissions and evidence are sparse.

propositions.text: Totality of Mr. Alabi's application was not sparse given his lengthy background with CIC before the decision maker.
propositions.quote: However, the totality of his application was not sparse given his lengthy background with CIC which was all before what he saw as the decision maker.

propositions.text: This is an exceptional circumstance and findings will be distinguishable due to the situation's distinctiveness.
propositions.quote: This is an exceptional circumstance and these findings will be distinguishable because of the distinctiveness of the situation.

paragraphs.summary: Some fault lies with Mr. Alabi for sparse evidence, but overall application was not sparse; this is an exceptional, distinctive circumstance.

propositions.text: One reason for Mr. Alabi's TRP application was his daughter's May 2016 convocation, which has passed.
propositions.quote: I note that one of the reasons Mr. Alabi applied for the TRP was the May 2016 convocation of his daughter. That date has since passed.

propositions.text: Mr. Alabi should be allowed to make new submissions on re-determination.
propositions.quote: Therefore in sending this back for re-determination, Mr. Alabi should be allowed to make new submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The daughter's May 2016 convocation has passed; Mr. Alabi should be allowed new submissions on re-determination.

propositions.text: The court is not indicating a TRP should be granted; that is for the decision maker after new evidence.
propositions.quote: I wish to be very clear that I am in no way indicating that a TRP should be granted as that is for the decision maker to decide after the Applicant has had an opportunity to file more evidence or at least update the application.

paragraphs.summary: The court clarifies it does not indicate a TRP grant; that decision is for the decision maker after new evidence.

propositions.text: Mr. Alabi argues for a directed verdict ordering CIC to issue a TRP, relying on Rudder and Singh.
propositions.quote: Mr. Alabi argued that I should issue a directed verdict by ordering CIC to issue him a TRP. He relies on Rudder, above, where Justice Lemieux granted such declaration and Singh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 757 [Singh].

propositions.text: In Rudder, Justice Lemieux found only reasonable outcome was granting a TRP.
propositions.quote: In Rudder, Justice Lemieux found that the only reasonable outcome the officer could reach on re-determination was the granting of a TRP.

propositions.text: This case is distinguishable; another officer may refuse TRP after full merits consideration.
propositions.quote: This case is distinguishable as it is open to another officer to refuse the TRP once the merits of the application are given full consideration.

propositions.text: This case differs from Singh where decision delay was 14 years due to lost passport; here delay is 8 years, not CIC error.
propositions.quote: This case is also distinguishable from Singh, above, in which the decision was not rendered for 14 years because CIC had lost the applicant’s passport. In this case, there has been an eight year delay which is long but not of a duration such as 14 years in Rudder and the delay is not a CIC induced error.

propositions.text: Facts do not justify directed verdict or mandamus; re-determination with possibility to file further evidence is sufficient remedy.
propositions.quote: These facts do not justify a directed verdict or mandamus. I find that an order for re-determination with the possibility for Mr. Alabi to file further evidence is a sufficient remedy.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Alabi seeks directed verdict citing Rudder and Singh; court finds case distinguishable and orders re-determination with evidence filing opportunity.

propositions.text: Reasonableness requires justification, transparency, intelligibility, and defensible outcomes (Dunsmuir; Khosa).
propositions.quote: Reasonableness requires that the decision must exhibit justification, transparency and intelligibility within the decision making process and also the decision must be within the range of possible, acceptable outcomes, defensible in fact and law (Dunsmuir; Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12)

propositions.text: Officer's decision is not reasonable for reasons stated; sent back for re-determination allowing new evidence and submissions.
propositions.quote: and for the reasons stated herein, I find that the officer’s decision is not reasonable. As such, I am sending it back for re-determination and will allow Mr. Alabi to file further evidence and submissions (hopefully utilizing counsel to do so).

propositions.text: Judicial review granted; matter sent back to different officer; applicant can file new evidence; fees waived; no question certified; no costs ordered.
propositions.quote: JUDGMENT THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The application for judicial review is granted and the matter is sent back to be re-determined by a different officer; The Applicant can file new evidence and/or written submissions. Any fees for this re-determination will be waived; No question is certified; No costs are ordered.

paragraphs.summary: Reasonableness requires defensible decisions; officer's decision is unreasonable; judicial review granted; matter remanded with new evidence allowed and fees waived.
